items.reason: The document lists testing business logic in contracts as an anti-pattern and its consumer tests assert only shape, status, and types.
Every response field in the consumer examples is wrapped in a matcher (like, eachLike, integer, string, regex), and the document explicitly instructs using Matchers.
The compose file injects DB_PASSWORD and PACT_BROKER_PASSWORD from the environment and the document warns that hardcoding them leaks secrets.
The document states never to skip can-i-deploy on main and both pipelines gate deployment on main.

items.text: one massive pact covering every endpoint
items.reason: The document lists one massive pact as an anti-pattern and advises starting with critical integration points incrementally.

items.text: business logic validation in contract test
items.reason: Business logic validation is called out as an anti-pattern; the contract tests only check status codes and field shapes.
State handlers seed and clear the database for each given state, and skipping provider states is listed as an anti-pattern.

items.text: hardcoded values instead of parameterized states
items.reason: All consumer interactions and the matching provider handler hardcode specific ids in state names (user 123, user 999) rather than using the parameterized state form the document only mentions as an aside.
The validateAgainstSpec helper throws on a missing schema and on validation failure with the Ajv errors included.
Response bodies in the consumer tests use matchers for every field rather than hardcoded literal values.

items.text: not using eachLike for array responses
items.reason: The paginated list example uses eachLike for the data array.
